topic: Alcohols, phenols and ethers — mixed tiers
description: Methanol, ethanol, glycol, glycerol, phenol, common ethers, IUPAC, denatured alcohol, exam-favourite uses

questions.stem: The functional group that defines an alcohol is:

options.option_text: Hydroxyl (−OH) attached to a saturated carbon

questions.explanation: ALCOHOL — −OH attached to an sp³ (saturated) carbon. R−OH. Examples: methanol CH₃OH, ethanol C₂H₅OH, propan-2-ol (isopropyl alcohol). PHENOL — −OH attached to an aromatic ring (sp² carbon of benzene); chemically distinct from alcohols (more acidic). ENOL — −OH on a C=C carbon (usually unstable). Alcohols are classified by the carbon bearing OH — primary (R−CH₂OH), secondary (R₂CHOH), tertiary (R₃COH).

questions.stem: Methanol (CH₃OH) is also called wood spirit because:

options.option_text: It is extracted from forest pine
It was historically obtained by destructive distillation of wood
It is used to polish wood

questions.explanation: Methanol — historic name 'wood alcohol' / 'wood spirit' because it was obtained by the destructive distillation of wood (pyrolysis without air). Modern industrial production: catalytic synthesis from CO + 2H₂ (syngas) over a Cu/ZnO/Al₂O₃ catalyst. Highly toxic — small ingestion causes blindness (optic-nerve damage by formate, the toxic metabolite produced by alcohol dehydrogenase + aldehyde dehydrogenase) and death. Treatment: ethanol or fomepizole (competitive inhibitors of ADH) + dialysis. Used as solvent, antifreeze, fuel, and precursor for formaldehyde, acetic acid, MTBE.

questions.stem: Ethanol used in industries is often 'denatured' by adding methanol or pyridine. The purpose is to:

options.option_text: Make it unfit for human consumption (so excise duty for industrial alcohol need not be paid as for potable alcohol)

questions.explanation: Denatured (or 'methylated') spirit — ethanol with poisonous additives (methanol, pyridine, denatonium benzoate — the bitterest substance known) so it cannot be drunk. This avoids the high excise duty levied on potable alcohol while allowing industrial use as solvent, fuel, cleaner. India's blending programme E20 — petrol with 20% ethanol; achieved Apr 2025 (5 years ahead of the 2030 target). Ethanol obtained from sugarcane molasses, broken rice, maize. Power alcohol = anhydrous ethanol blended with petrol.

questions.stem: Glycerol (glycerine) is a tri-hydric alcohol with 3 −OH groups. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.explanation: Glycerol — HOCH₂−CHOH−CH₂OH; IUPAC name propane-1,2,3-triol. Sweet, viscous, non-toxic; used in cosmetics, soaps (glycerol is a byproduct of soap-making by saponification of fats), pharmaceuticals (cough syrups, suppositories), foods (humectant E422), nitroglycerine (explosive — Alfred Nobel's dynamite, 1867). Propan-1-ol — CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (mono-hydric). Propan-2-ol — IPA, isopropyl alcohol, used in hand sanitiser. Ethane-1,2-diol — ethylene glycol (HOCH₂CH₂OH), antifreeze, polyester (PET) precursor.

questions.stem: Phenol (C₆H₅OH) is more acidic than ethanol primarily because:

options.option_text: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance / delocalisation of the negative charge into the benzene ring
Phenol forms hydrogen bonds with water

questions.explanation: Phenol pKa ≈ 10; ethanol pKa ≈ 16 — phenol is ~10⁶ times more acidic than ethanol. Reason: when phenol loses H⁺, the resulting phenoxide ion (C₆H₅O⁻) has the negative charge delocalised over the aromatic ring (resonance into ortho/para positions). Ethoxide (C₂H₅O⁻) has the negative charge localised on oxygen — less stable. EWGs (NO₂, CN, X) on the ring increase acidity of phenols (ortho/para positions especially); EDGs (CH₃, OCH₃, NH₂) decrease acidity. Used as an antiseptic (Joseph Lister, 1865) — though largely replaced; now used to make Bakelite, aspirin, paracetamol, dyes.

questions.stem: Diethyl ether (C₂H₅−O−C₂H₅), an early surgical anaesthetic, has the general formula R−O−R′. Ethers are characterised by:

options.option_text: An oxygen atom bonded to two carbon (alkyl/aryl) groups

questions.explanation: Ether — R−O−R′. The two R groups can be the same (symmetrical: dimethyl ether, diethyl ether) or different (asymmetrical: methyl ethyl ether). Diethyl ether — used as a surgical anaesthetic (William Morton, 1846) — replaced by safer agents (halothane, isoflurane). Highly volatile + flammable. Methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE) — petrol additive (octane booster, replaced tetraethyl lead). Cellosolve — ethylene glycol monoethyl ether, industrial solvent. Crown ethers — cyclic polyethers, complex with metal cations (used for selective ion extraction).

questions.stem: The 'absolute alcohol' used in laboratories refers to:

options.option_text: Anhydrous ethanol — ethanol containing essentially no water (>99.5%)

questions.explanation: Ordinary distillation of fermented broth gives ~95.6% ethanol — an azeotrope with water (boils 78.2 °C). To get above 99.5% ('absolute alcohol'), one must break the azeotrope: (1) Drying agents like CaO (quicklime); (2) Azeotropic distillation with benzene (older industrial method); (3) Molecular sieves (zeolites) — modern + safer. Used in spectroscopy, in the lab as a non-aqueous solvent, in pharma, as fuel-grade ethanol. Rectified spirit ≈ 95% ethanol; methylated spirit ≈ 95% ethanol + 5% methanol; surgical spirit ≈ 70% ethanol with castor oil + methanol — the 70% concentration is most effective at killing microbes (water + ethanol both needed to disrupt cells).
